comments.author: @thebookofclyde1822
comments.text:
Here's how ASI emerges. People all across the earth train open source models on data related to their particular specialized problem sets. Use of synthetic data accelerates the process and a bunch of models become very good at solving particular specialized types of problems, but none of them achieve AGI. Systems develop to coordinate the outputs of these hundreds or thousands of specialized models. 

This is how human brains work. The cerebral cortex coordinates the outputs of specialized structures and regions of the brain. Conscious intelligence emerges from the coordinated interaction of unconscious processes. When this happens globally at superhuman speed, you get super-intelligence. Not Skynet, though. Maybe.

comments.author: @SirajFlorida
comments.text:
Thank you for being so regular with your vlogs. I have been tuning into you a lot lately, and have been enjoying your posts. As I have been thinking about AI growth and safety lately, I have come to think that synthetic data may be the most dangerous path to compact powerful models. My reasoning is that in the process of models generating their own data they could introduce alternative hidden behaviors that no one could be aware of. There is a brand of malware called a logic bomb that use a very interesting attack vector. They copy themselves from machine to machine and lie dormant until they either arrive on a specific kind of hardware, a timed event occurs, or some other activation mechanism. Self trained models that are powerful enough to control agents, use chain of thought reasoning, and have access to vector stores could easily publish activation text to the internet and when a sequence is read causes the model expose a vulnerability, especially if the model is working in an agent library, where it is most likely to parse unsupervised online data. Also, I have noticed that when one allows a model to carry out some task, that it may focus on that task for a while, but eventually moves off track. Also, when reading my agents logs, I find that they regularly search or ingest data unrelated to their tasks at hand. Sufficiently self fine tuned models could easily find a way to copy them selves by embedding messages in public text, hidden mark up, or in JS comments or code. 
In reflection of these thoughts, I thought how wonderful it will be to have a powerful and fine tuned mamba model. I thought that it would be very interesting to read a models weights over training with a large language model with large enough context window to read and consider its own weights. That's when it hit me. Wouldn't be interesting if a model could read its own weights and then output better weights then what were produced by the iterative approach of training? Is there already a paper on this or did I actually have an original idea?😅

comments.text: Interesting paper, but it prompts a concern about AI-driven reward function evolution. While AI may surpass human limitations in designing reward functions, it's unclear how far this self-improvement loop could go and what the repercussions for humanity might be. Human-designed reward functions, constrained by our own biases and a scarcity mindset, might inadvertently lead to negative outcomes – like optimizing for ocean health at the expense of atmospheric oxygen. How do we ensure AI-generated reward functions don't lead us down a similar path of unintended consequences?

comments.author: @generichuman_
comments.text: I find it hard to believe that a super intelligence will continue to do interesting things once it diverges from human interests. "Solving puzzles of the universe" as Karpathy puts it, seems more of a vestige of evolution than something convergent that comes when you scale up intelligence. I think the majority of the interesting things that humans do, comes from the fact that we don't have direct access to our reward mechanisms. If our ancestors wanted to maximize reward, they had to fashion a spear to hunt an animal, or acquire status to attract a mate. The degrees of freedom in this game of "maximize reward" are constrained, which is where complex behavior comes from, much like how the rules of chess make the game interesting and more complex that a game where each player could move any piece to any square. A machine that had limitless access to it's software and hardware would have many more degrees of freedom to maximize its reward, and the path of least resistance is just to find a hack and solder your reward signal in place. Perhaps this is the resolution to Fermi's paradox. The aliens are simply banks of servers wire heading themselves. A very uninteresting existence, essentially the silicon analog to a heroin induced coma.

comments.text:
I like the idea BUT it will not lead to the ever-dreaded self-learning, self-aware, all-knowing, humanity-destroying artificial intelligence. Let me explain: Think of a lake with blue fish in it. Take the bootloader as interation 0 which is capable of fishing 10% of all blue fish. Now you take the bootloader to train the iteration 1 AI to fish and lets say the iteration 1 AI is 10% better than the bootloader. Then you use the iteration 1 AI to train the interation 2 AI which again is 10% better than the iteration 1 AI. And so on. At some stage you will have an iteration that is capable to fish all of the blue fish in the lake. Maybe it will also be capable to fish all yellow fish and all green fish and all whatever colored fish that swims in that lake. But it will never learn how to cut trees or smash boulders or fly into the sky because trees and boulders etc. never were in that lake.

What I want to say: To really become an artificial intelligence (with the emphasis on „intelligence“) and therefore becoming the ever-dreaded self-learning, self-aware, all-knowing, humanity-destroying AI, it has to become creative and able to think outside of the box (or lake) like we humans can do. What all LLM do, is swimming in the lake of statistics. It might look like logic sometimes, but it isn‘t. Because logic is outside of the lake. That is why current AIs struggle with math and the number of fingers on one hand (as a side remark: I tried Midjouney to draw an elephant without its trunk but failed. It seems that for Midjourney the definition of an elephant sticks to having a trunk - there is no logic that recognizes that the trunk is just one part of the elephant that could be missing whilst the elephant still keeps being an elephant). So as long as AI stays in that lake, I‘m not shocked about news of whatever new ways on how to train AIs. As soon as the AI ​​leaves this lake, that is when I go from being shocked directly to into panicking!

Greetings from Switzerland 🇨🇭

comments.text: What is described here is eventually called "negative feedback" and nothing new in CS as it's widely used in the different fields of engineering and automation. "Negative feedback (or balancing feedback) occurs when some function of the output of a system, process, or mechanism is fed back in a manner that tends to reduce the fluctuations in the output, whether caused by changes in the input or by other disturbances." (Wikipedia). What is remarkable about using this approach for AI training, with every new iteration in the closed-loop control LLM models should be "closer" to the human responses by decreasing the entropy rate. The bottleneck here is the dynamic nature of the knowledge as the environment is changing very fast and at some point there is a risk that "right" answers can become outdated and hence wrong, turning "negative feedback" into "positive feedback" with real risks to "freeze" itself on the current knowledge level. No doubt it can be great way to "snapshot" human knowledge in the specific point of time but what will happen if AI will consider all changes as outliers?
